key_findings.detail: IC5 Staff: 'I set the multi-year, multi-team technical strategy'; influences roadmaps of OTHER teams; favors 'priorities of the wider engineering org rather than locally optimal outcomes'; leads decisions 'even when making unpopular decisions.' IC6 Principal: 'org/company-wide multi-year goals,' 'transcend organizational boundaries,' partners with Directors/senior EPD leadership, handles decisions with 'no one clearly correct answer' whose consequences are 'sweeping.' CRITICAL: on both, 'The expectations for code fluency do not go beyond L4' and software design plateaus at L5. Growth above is scope, strategy authority, leadership tier, and talent development — NOT deeper coding.
key_findings.why_it_matters: This is the hardest evidence for level-up's core value prop. It lets the platform tell learners bluntly: getting better at coding will NOT get you promoted past Senior — and back it with a Big Tech public ladder.

key_findings.finding: Reilly's 'Being Glue' names the career trap: invisible integrative work that keeps teams shipping but doesn't get you promoted
key_findings.detail: Glue work = noticing the broken process and fixing it, mentoring, writing the docs, reviewing designs, coordinating projects, onboarding, unblocking others. Reilly's argument: this work is essential but 'non-promotable' — it's often not on the ladder criteria, and disproportionately falls on women and underrepresented engineers, crowding out the technical work promotion committees actually reward. Advice: do glue work with eyes open, be deliberate about how much, ensure your core technical/strategic contributions remain visible, and negotiate to make the leadership work your actual recognized role rather than an invisible tax. Larson's StaffEng deliberately defers to this essay rather than 'a watery rehash.'
key_findings.why_it_matters: level-up must teach glue work as a double-edged sword — coach learners to do it strategically and make it visible, not just do more of it. A blind spot for many stalled Seniors.

key_findings.finding: Sponsorship (Lara Hogan) beats mentorship for advancing others — and it is a gradable Staff+ behavior
key_findings.detail: Mentorship = giving advice; sponsorship = 'feeling on the hook to help get someone promoted,' spending your own capital. Concrete sponsorship behaviors: suggest someone as lead on a new project, recommend them as postmortem facilitator, forward their work email to a new audience 'underscoring why it was interesting,' cite their insight to influential groups, get them a talk/blog post. Underrepresented engineers usually need 'opportunity and visibility,' not more advice. Sponsorship can be invisible — 'you can sponsor someone without them even knowing it.' Larson echoes: effective Staff engineers use 'considerably more sponsorship' than mentorship.
key_findings.why_it_matters: The 'Leveling Up Others' axis should score sponsorship specifically, not generic mentoring. Gives concrete, observable behaviors to assess and coach toward.

key_findings.finding: Charity Majors' engineer/manager pendulum reframes the IC track as a first-class, non-terminal path
key_findings.detail: 'Fuck the whole idea that only managers get career progression.' 'Management is NOT a promotion... it's a change of profession.' 'The best frontline eng managers are never more than 2-3 years removed from hands-on work.' A tech lead 'IS a manager' (prioritizes the task over people) who needs the full manager toolset. Advocates swinging between IC and management serially (not simultaneously — the hybrid is 'an unstable combination' because deep eng requires blocking interruptions while management is interruptive). Draining senior engineers into management robs orgs of 'the great mentors and elder wizards we need.'
key_findings.why_it_matters: level-up should position the Staff+ IC track as equal to management and teach management-adjacent skills (running projects, influence, the 'manager toolset') without requiring a management title.

key_findings.finding: The defining experiential shift is the FEEDBACK LOOP, not the skill list
key_findings.detail: StaffEng: the core challenge of operating at Staff is 'a much slower feedback cycle' — replacing the immediate 'coding REPL' with 'the uneven progress of mentorship, relationship building, and strategy'; feedback loops stretch to weeks, months, years. Katie Sylor-Miller: the myth that you'll be 'in control of the work you do and everyone will listen to you' is 'the opposite of what happens.' Joy Ebertz: 'the more senior you get, the less your job is about code.'
key_findings.why_it_matters: level-up must set expectations that Staff+ growth feels slow and ambiguous, and design its own feedback/practice loops to compensate — e.g. simulations and scenario judgment rather than code-graded exercises.

key_findings.finding: Influence-without-authority has concrete named sub-skills in the StaffEng canon
key_findings.detail: 'Stay aligned with authority' — Staff leadership runs on 'proxied authority from a (usually managerial) leader,' so you must be 'aligned, trustworthy, and predictable.' 'To lead, you have to follow' — 'blend your vision with the visions of your peers and leadership.' 'Learn to never be wrong' — shift 'towards understanding and communication' rather than winning, to avoid spending social capital 'repairing relationships frayed by conflict.' 'Build a network of peers' to vet decisions once authority starts to 'temper feedback.' 'Create space for others.'
key_findings.why_it_matters: Influence is often treated as a soft platitude; StaffEng decomposes it into 5 teachable, assessable behaviors that can become roadmap modules.

key_findings.finding: Larson's 'Work on What Matters' gives a concrete anti-pattern taxonomy for judgment/prioritization
key_findings.detail: Avoid: Snacking (easy low-impact work), Preening (low-impact HIGH-visibility work — requires 'near invulnerability to criticism of your actual impact'), Chasing ghosts (high-effort low-impact, common when new leaders 'misjudge the familiar as the essential'). Focus instead on: Existential issues (companies run 'iterative elimination tournaments'), work with 'room and attention,' Glue work, Fostering growth ('your legacy'), Editing (small high-leverage changes), Finishing things ('we only get value from finishing projects'), and 'what only you can do.'
key_findings.why_it_matters: This is a ready-made rubric for the judgment/prioritization axis — learners can be given scenarios and scored on whether they snack/preen/chase ghosts vs. pick existential/high-leverage work.

key_findings.finding: Writing is a load-bearing Staff+ skill, not a nice-to-have — strategy docs and RFCs are the primary artifacts of influence
key_findings.detail: StaffEng lists 'Writing engineering strategy' as a core operating skill: a doc guiding how the org supports business objectives via 'architecture, technology selection, and organizational structure.' Reilly Ch3 is a whole chapter on writing technical vision/strategy docs (approach-write-launch). Reilly's Squarespace RFC work shows the mechanism: an 'opinionated RFC template' with named approvers who say 'yes' or 'yes, if' (not gate-keeping 'no'), plus a small Architecture Review (~10 people, 50 min discuss / 10 min decide, 'rough consensus') — used for org-wide decisions like adopting Go and gRPC.
key_findings.why_it_matters: level-up should make written artifacts (strategy docs, RFCs, design proposals) a graded deliverable — arguably the single most transferable, evidenceable Staff+ skill.

key_findings.finding: Gergely Orosz confirms the Staff+ title hierarchy and that Senior is the terminal/'career' level at most companies
key_findings.detail: Staff+ hierarchy above Senior: 'Staff, Senior Staff, Principal, Senior Principal, Distinguished or Fellow.' Staff is 'the level which follows senior engineer at Big Tech' for ICs 'of greater scope than senior.' levels.fyi corroborates Senior as 'the career level' where most engineers spend their careers and never need to progress further; Staff is <10%, Principal is 'very few.'
key_findings.why_it_matters: Frames level-up's market honestly: going Senior->Staff+ is a minority path requiring a deliberate behavioral change, which justifies a dedicated platform rather than generic upskilling.

implications_for_build: Base the assessment's 5 axes on the convergent industry framework rather than inventing one. Recommended: (1) Scope & Blast Radius, (2) Judgment Under Ambiguity, (3) Technical Direction & Strategy (incl. writing), (4) Influence Without Authority, (5) Leveling Up Others (sponsorship). This maps cleanly onto Reilly's 3 pillars + Larson's 5 responsibilities + the levels.fyi/Dropbox axes, so it is externally defensible.

Score each axis on a Senior/Staff/Principal band using the exact public-ladder descriptors: Senior = immediate-team blast radius, low-moderate ambiguity, hands-on; Staff = multi-team, design over implementation, moderate-high ambiguity; Principal = org/multi-org, fully autonomous, highest ambiguity, rarely codes. This gives learners a concrete, credible 'you are here' verdict.

Lead the product narrative with the Dropbox 'code fluency plateaus at L4' fact. level-up's core promise should be explicit: coding skill will not promote you past Senior — we train the judgment/leverage/direction that does. This is a sharp, evidence-backed differentiator vs. LeetCode/coding-course competitors.

Do NOT grade primarily on code. Because Staff+ has weeks-to-years feedback loops and is about judgment, build the assessment around scenario/situational-judgment items and written artifacts (strategy docs, RFCs, prioritization calls) rather than auto-graded coding exercises.

Make written artifacts a first-class graded deliverable: a technical strategy doc (Reilly Ch3 approach-write-launch) and an RFC using a yes/'yes, if' approver model (Reilly's Squarespace pattern). This is the most transferable and evidenceable Staff+ skill.

Turn Larson's 'Work on What Matters' taxonomy into a prioritization mini-assessment: present realistic backlogs and score whether the learner snacks/preens/chases ghosts vs. targets existential and high-leverage work. This directly measures the judgment axis.

Diagnose and let learners choose an archetype (Tech Lead / Architect / Solver / Right Hand). Each archetype needs a distinct roadmap — a Solver's path (deep problem-solving, transience) differs sharply from a Tech Lead's (team, PM partnership, delegation). One-size-fits-all roadmap would be wrong.

Build a dedicated 'Leveling Up Others' module that teaches sponsorship as distinct from mentorship, with Hogan's concrete behaviors (amplify in rooms they're not in, hand off stretch/lead work, cite their work to influential groups) as gradable actions.

Include an explicit 'Being Glue' coaching module: teach learners to identify glue work, do it strategically, keep core technical/strategic contributions visible, and negotiate leadership work into their recognized role. Critical for stalled Seniors, especially women/underrepresented engineers.

Position the Staff+ IC track as equal to management (Charity Majors) and teach the 'manager toolset' (running big projects, influence-without-authority, stakeholder alignment) without requiring a management title — this defines level-up's lane.

Set expectations in onboarding that Staff+ growth feels slow and ambiguous with delayed feedback, and design the platform's own tight practice/feedback loops (simulations, peer review, scenario replays) to counteract the naturally long real-world feedback cycle.
